summary: The AGI calculator works out real estate/rental income and losses from the salary, wages and tips, the business / self-employment, the interest, dividends, royalties, etc. and the capital gains and losses. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the AGI calculator work?
sections.html:
The AGI calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports real estate/rental income and losses in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the salary, wages and tips, the business / self-employment, the interest, dividends, royalties, etc. and the capital gains and losses.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the AGI calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Real estate/rental income and losses=-spousal support ÷ Alimony received − pension ÷ Annuity ÷ IRA distributions − awards ÷ prizes ÷ winnings − business ÷ self-employment − capital gains and losses + gross income − interest, dividends, royalties, etc. − jury duty fees − other income − social security benefits − taxable state refunds − unemployment compensation − salary, wages and tips
Contributions to retirement / IRAs=-alimony paid − educator expenses − health insurance premiums − healthcare savings account (HSA) contributions − moving expenses − other deductions − retirement plan contributions − school tuition − half of self-employment tax − student loan interest + total adjustments to income
Gross income=adjusted gross income + total adjustments to income

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The AGI calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the salary, wages and tips, the business / self-employment and the interest, dividends, royalties, etc. — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the AGI calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns real estate/rental income and losses, derived from the salary, wages and tips, the business / self-employment and the interest, dividends, royalties, etc.. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the AGI calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the salary, wages and tips, the business / self-employment, the interest, dividends, royalties, etc. and the capital gains and losses, which is 26 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter salary, wages and tips in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Salary, wages and tips opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Gross income = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the AGI calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
